Article Title: Former NASA specialist claims he has found a way to overcome Earth's gravity in a 'major discovery'
Article Text: A former NASA engineer claims he has found a way to overcome Earth's gravity, and all ears have perked up. Exodus Propulsion Technologies, a private company co-founded by Charles Buhler, an electrostatics specialist has made the claim, according to a report by Popular Mechanics. With Buhler having worked for NASA and Kennedy Space Centre, his words have made for an extremely interesting pedigree.Previously, Buhler has helped establish the Electrostatics and Surface Physics Laboratory at Kennedy Space Centre in Florida, a very important lab that ensures rockets don't explode. He is a veteran of storied programs such as NASA’s Space Shuttle, the International Space Station (ISS), The Hubble Telescope, and the current NASA Dust Program. Now, with his own company, he has argued that his team has found a propellantless effect driven by electric fields, a 'New Force' that can generate enough thrust to counter gravity, as he described it to The Debrief.“The most important message to convey to the public is that a major discovery occurred,” Buhler told The Debrief. “This discovery of a New Force is fundamental in that electric fields alone can generate a sustainable force onto an object and allow centre-of-mass translation of said object without expelling mass.”In an interview with APEC’s co-founder Tim Ventura, Buhler explained how his background in electrostatics led to the discovery. He says his team, made up of people from NASA, Blue Origin, and the Air Force, investigated propellant-less drives for two decades before arriving at electrostatics. “Nature has its own way of doing things,” Buhler explained, “and it is our job to uncover what nature does. It just happened to fall into my lap in what I’m the expert in. ”For years, their devices produced negligible thrust, but saw increases with each new iteration. For example, from 2016 to the end of 2020, their best devices were producing a little more than one hundred thousandth of a gravity. In the coming years, that would go up exponentially. For clarification, Buhler said that measuring thrust in terms of a percentage of gravity reflects the force generated divided by the test article.“The aim is to approach and exceed unity,” he explained, “which means the article would generate enough thrust to lift itself in Earth’s gravity, and that’s defined as 1 gravity of thrust.”Buhler says they commonly measured the forces in milliNewtons, but they prefer to describe the thrust in terms of gravity since that is the ultimate goal of propulsion physics. “The highest we have generated on a stacked system is about 10 mN,” he said. “The magnitude is not important, really, since anything above zero would work in space!”In the years and months leading up to the breakthrough thrust measurement, Buhler and his team took great care to methodically eliminate anything else that could account for the tiny yet measurable force they were seeing. This detailed and painstaking work resulted in the team’s overriding patent, which was granted in 2020.With fresh momentum, Buhler says they also began construction of a custom-made vacuum chamber that would allow them to simulate the environment of deep space. If something else was causing the force, this chamber was built to identify it.According to the APEC presentation, that chamber was completed at the end of 2020. Between January and September 2021, 146 separate articles were tested, each seemingly confirming the presence of measurable thrust. The team also tested different configurations that eliminated the old designs using asymmetrical capacitors and instead employed models with opposing asymmetrical plates.Then, in 2022, something astounding happened. According to Buhler, his team began to see significant jumps in the force being generated. A quick look at a chart he presented to APEC shows that tests performed between early 2022 and November 2023 resulted in a rapid climb, moving from one thousandth, one hundredth, and even one-tenth of gravity all the way up to one full Earth gravity. This means that their current devices, which Buhler told “weigh somewhere between 30-40 grams on their own” without the attached test equipment, were producing enough thrust to counteract the full force of one Earth gravity. This culminated in 2023, when this “New Force”-powered drive generated enough thrust to overcome Earth’s gravity.After decades of research, Buhler says he and his team had shown unequivocally that a new, fundamental force was at work and that his devices were tapping into that force to produce thrust without emitting any mass or propellant.“Essentially, what we’ve discovered is that systems that contain an asymmetry in either electrostatic pressure or some kind of electrostatic divergent field can give a system of a centre of mass a non-zero force component,” Buhler explained. “So, what that basically means is that there’s some underlying physics that can essentially place force on an object should those two constraints be met.”APEC event listings in January, March, and May 2026 described continued “testing and refinement” by Exodus co-founder Andrew Aurigema. In a March 2026 interview, Buhler said he had run roughly 2,000 vacuum-chamber experiments and was emphasising effects such as thrust that allegedly persisted after power was turned off.Buhler stressed that this work is unaffiliated with NASA. Much of the public discussion has moved through the Alternative Propulsion Energy Conference, or APEC, a community built around advanced-propulsion ideas that range from serious engineering questions to claims that still need far more careful testing.Exodus has also moved into a more openly investor-facing phase. An official Deep Tech Week NYC 2026 listing advertised an “Exodus Propulsion Technologies - Meet and Greet” on April 4, inviting physicists and investors to discuss the technology and meet Buhler as CEO/founder.As of May 2026, there isn’t a published independent replication using an outside lab’s own apparatus, instrumentation, and uncertainty budget.Previously, in 2001, British Electrical Engineer Roger Shawyer first introduced the “impossible drive,” known as the EmDrive. It earned that nickname because Shawyer claimed it could produce thrust without propellant. The EmDrive spent years producing tantalising little signals, including a reported thrust measurement from NASA’s Eagleworks team in 2016. Then better tests caught up. By 2021, work at the Dresden University of Technology found no thrust from the device, turning one of the most famous propellantless-drive claims into a cautionary tale about tiny forces, experimental noise, and wishful machinery.Up next, Buhler says his team is seeking funding to test their devices in space to better understand the force at work.“We’re hoping to do some demos,” said Buhler. “Some space demos. That’s what we’re trying to get some funding to do. I think that would be a great way to show off the technology.”
Article Summary: Exodus Propulsion Technologies is a private company co-founded by Charles Buhler, an electrostatics specialist. Previously, he worked for NASA and the Kennedy Space Centre in Florida. He says his team has found a propellantless effect driven by electric fields, a 'New Force' that can generate enough thrust to counter gravity.

Article Title: At 21, an Australian artist bought 25 acres in Tasmania; 18 months later a bushfire destroyed her first home, so she rebuilt it from salvage materials into an off-grid cabin for AU$7,000-10,000
Article Text:
She Bought 25 Acres at 21. After the Bushfire, She Built This Cabin From What Survived

Bushfire destruction led to a low-cost rebuild

Off-grid systems keep living costs low

Tasmania cabin reflects wider interest in alternative homes

An Australian artist who used her savings to buy a 25-acre bush block in Tasmania at the age of 21 has built an off-grid home using salvaged materials after a bushfire destroyed her original house just 18 months after she moved in. After losing her first home and having limited money left, she decided not to use a traditional homebuilder. Instead, she spent months collecting discarded timber, metal sheets and old building materials from salvage yards and fire-damaged sites across the island. She used them to build a self-contained cabin for an estimated AU$7,000 to AU$10,000. According to a feature published by alternative housing publication Tiny House Talk, the project shows how using salvaged materials can provide a low-cost way to build a home, especially for young Australians facing high housing costs and increasing environmental risks. The rebuilt home is completely off the electricity and water grids. It uses rooftop solar panels, battery storage and rainwater tanks to meet the owner's basic needs in the remote Tasmanian countryside.The artist originally bought the land to create a studio and get away from rising rents in cities. Just 18 months after moving in, a bushfire swept through the area, destroying her first home and much of the surrounding vegetation.Instead of leaving the property or taking on a large mortgage, she decided to rebuild using cheaper and recycled materials, a method highlighted by independent housing publications such as Tiny House Talk. She collected structural timber, corrugated iron sheets and secondhand glass windows to build a small, single-storey cabin. Friends and local tradespeople also helped with heavy work and some specialist electrical connections. The design focuses on keeping the cabin warm and making it better able to withstand fire. Metal sheets on the outside provide a non-combustible layer, while the windows were positioned to make better use of sunlight for heating during Tasmania's cold winters. Inside, reclaimed wooden floorboards and reused timber panels were used for much of the interior. This helped reduce building costs while giving old materials another use instead of sending them to landfill.The cabin uses its own power and water systems instead of relying on public utilities. These systems were designed to work with Tasmania's changing weather conditions. Electricity comes from a small solar panel system connected to a deep-cycle battery bank. It provides enough power for LED lights, refrigeration and charging electronic devices. Cooking is done using bottled gas and a traditional cast-iron wood-burning stove, which also provides the main source of heat during winter. Water comes from rainwater collected from the cabin's metal roof. The water flows into storage tanks, passes through filters and is then fed into the kitchen and bathroom through gravity. A dry composting toilet removes the need for a septic tank or connection to a public sewer system. This cuts both installation costs and future maintenance expenses. By keeping the initial building cost below AU$10,000 and avoiding regular utility bills, the owner has kept her monthly costs low. This has allowed her to focus on her art without the financial pressure of a traditional mortgage.The project is part of a wider interest in alternative housing in Australia, where high property prices and interest rates have encouraged some people to consider smaller homes, recycled materials and off-grid technology. Building industry reports show growing interest in options such as tiny houses on wheels, converted shipping containers and self-built timber cabins, particularly in rural areas where land can be cheaper than in major cities. However, alternative housing projects can face planning and safety challenges. Local council rules and strict fire regulations can make it difficult to obtain approval for homes built with unusual designs or salvaged materials, especially in areas at high risk of bushfires. The completed Tasmanian cabin shows how careful design and the use of reclaimed materials can help property owners rebuild after extreme weather without taking on large amounts of debt. The owner continues to look after her 25-acre bush block, allowing native vegetation to grow back around the cabin while living full-time in the home she built herself.
Article Summary: Australian artist bought a 25-acre bush block in Tasmania at the age of 21. Just 18 months after moving in, a bushfire destroyed her first home. Instead of leaving the property or taking on a large mortgage, she decided to rebuild using cheaper and recycled materials. She spent months collecting discarded timber, metal sheets and old building materials from salvage yards and fire-damaged sites. She used them to build a self-contained cabin for an estimated AU$7,000 to AU$10,000.

Article Title: ‘Western troops in Ukraine would mean war with Russia’: Putin ahead of Brics meet
Article Text:
We are not threatening European countries, nor are we going to threaten them. Why would we?" Putin said (Photo: PTI).

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Saturday warned that discussions about deploying foreign troops to Ukraine would effectively amount to a declaration of war against Russia.Speaking on the sidelines of the Brics Summit, Putin remarked, "Now they are talking about how they are thinking about bringing troops to the territory of Ukraine. This means war with Russia."Addressing suggestions that Russia poses a threat to European nations amid the ongoing war in Ukraine, the Russian leader firmly rejected the notion."There is no such threat, and there has never been. We are not threatening European countries, nor are we going to threaten them. Why would we?" Putin said.He argued that there was no basis for any dispute between Russia and Europe, stating that all outstanding matters had been resolved following the second world war.Putin's remarks arrive as the war with Ukraine continues in its fifth year. Since then, several European countries have continued to back Ukraine, while the United States has sought to play the role of mediator, facilitating talks between Moscow and Kyiv.Turning to political developments within Europe, Putin also commented on the recent rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party, which topped the state election in Saxony-Anhalt earlier this month.He described the current state of affairs across Europe as the outcome of "systemic mistakes" made by the West in the fields of politics, security and economics."Everyone makes mistakes. We have made quite a few mistakes ourselves, as has the rest of the world," Putin acknowledged, before adding that the West's "globalists" had, since the end of the Cold War and the fall of the Soviet Union, come to see themselves as being at the "top of Olympus", believing both that they could act without constraint and that they were incapable of error.According to exit poll figures released by German broadcaster ARD and reported by Al Jazeera, the AfD won 44.5 per cent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, more than double the 18.5 per cent secured by Chancellor Friedrich Merz's centre-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU).This marks the first time since the Second World War that a far-right party has come first in a German state election.The AfD has never been part of a governing coalition at either state or federal level, with mainstream parties upholding a long-standing refusal to work with it, a barrier widely known as the "firewall".
Article Summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin warns that deploying foreign troops to Ukraine would effectively amount to a declaration of war against Russia. Speaking on the sidelines of the Brics Summit, Putin remarked, "Now they are talking about how they are thinking about bringing troops to the territory of Ukraine. This means war with Russia."

Article Title: Around AD 310, a Roman emperor had a private bath built with three pools, heated floors and a sauna; archaeologists have now uncovered its unusual design
Article Text:
The bath was incorporated directly into the emperor’s palace, with its heating system, bathing areas and sophisticated architecture working together within a relatively compact space.

A palace built for an emperor

A bath unlike the usual Roman model

The bath, known in Latin as a balneum, was divided into two main areas.

Heated floors and three bathing pools

A glimpse into imperial life

Nearly 1,700 years ago, an emperor could retreat from the demands of the Roman court without leaving his palace. Beneath a monumental tower in what is now eastern Serbia, he had a private bathing suite built with heated floors, multiple pools and a sauna, a remarkably sophisticated space designed for comfort, privacy and relaxation. Archaeologists have now uncovered the remains of that unusual bath complex, offering a glimpse into the luxurious lifestyle of Roman Emperor Maximinus Daza and the engineering behind his imperial residence.The discovery was made at Vrelo-Šarkamen, a fortified residential complex constructed in the early fourth century. The site is associated with Maximinus Daza, who ruled as Roman emperor from 310 to 313. Excavations at the site have continued intermittently for decades, but recent work by researchers from Serbia’s Institute of Archaeology has revealed that the palace was considerably more elaborate than previously understood.Maximinus Daza, whose full name was Galerius Valerius Maximinus, was born in the region and rose to power during one of the most turbulent periods of the Roman Empire. He was part of the tetrarchy, a system established by Emperor Diocletian in which the vast empire was governed by four rulers. The arrangement was already beginning to unravel by the time Maximinus became emperor. His reign lasted only a few years, ending with his defeat by his rival Licinius and his death in 313.The most intriguing discovery lies beneath a monumental tower at the southwest corner of the palace. Rather than following the more familiar linear arrangement found in many Roman bathhouses, with rooms placed one after another, this private bath was circular and occupied the lowest level of the tower. Its unusual layout appears to have been carefully adapted to the architecture of the building. The room was covered by a dome fitted with six windows, an architectural feature that would have required considerable technical skill. The design also allowed the bath to combine practical infrastructure with an enclosed space intended for the emperor and other members of the palace elite.The bath, known in Latin as a balneum, was divided into two main areas. One section housed the equipment needed to keep the complex running. Archaeologists found the remains of a furnace that would have heated the floors, a hallmark of Roman bathing technology. They also uncovered the base of a copper boiler used to heat water, although the boiler itself has disappeared. The second section was devoted to bathing and relaxation. Inside, researchers found three bathing pools or tubs, along with a sudatorium, a room designed for steam bathing or sauna-like relaxation. Together, the features point to a space that was about far more than basic hygiene.For the Roman elite, bathing could be an important part of daily life, combining relaxation, socialising and personal care. In this case, however, the setting suggests something more private and exclusive. The bath was incorporated directly into the emperor’s palace, with its heating system, bathing areas and sophisticated architecture working together within a relatively compact space. Its position inside the tower also raises questions about how Maximinus Daza and his family reached the complex.Archaeologists plan to continue investigating the site, hoping to reconstruct the arrangement of the rooms and understand how the bath functioned within the wider palace.What survives at Vrelo-Šarkamen is more than a collection of ancient walls. It is a snapshot of imperial life at a moment when the Roman world was changing rapidly, preserved beneath a tower where an emperor once had the luxury of disappearing into his own private bath.Images Courtesy: Vrelo-Šarkamen research team/Institute of Archaeology
Article Summary: Archaeologists have uncovered the remains of a Roman bath complex. It offers a glimpse into the luxurious lifestyle of Roman Emperor Maximinus Daza. He had a private bathing suite built with heated floors, multiple pools and a sauna. The bath was incorporated directly into the emperor’s palace.

Article Title: In 1958, New Zealand built a power station over a volcanic field; it became the world's first to generate electricity from geothermal flash steam
Article Text:
Wairākei geothermal field in July 1978. Image Credit: Engineering New Zealand

How did New Zealand’s Wairākei power station become the world’s first to use flash steam

Wairākei Geothermal Power Station, Taupō District [22 August 1963]. Image Credit: Engineering New Zealand

The project turned underground heat into a practical power source

Why was Wairākei important to the field of geothermal engineering

The power station grew beyond its original development

Wairākei became part of New Zealand’s engineering heritage

Wairākei Power Station in New Zealand changed the way geothermal heat could be turned into electricity when it was commissioned in 1958. Built beside the Waikato River, north of Taupō, the station drew on hot underground water beneath an active volcanic zone. Instead of relying on conventional fuel, engineers drilled wells into the geothermal field and used the pressure of the heated water to produce steam for turbines. According to Engineering New Zealand, the project became the first in the world to use flash steam from geothermal water to generate electricity.Wairākei sits within an active volcanic zone stretching about 250 kilometres long and around 50 kilometres wide, narrowing to about 15 kilometres at either end. The station itself was built beside the Waikato River, roughly 10 kilometres north of Taupō, while its geothermal wells were drilled in the nearby Waiora Valley.The idea behind the project was relatively straightforward, even though putting it into practice required major engineering work. Deep underground was a vast water system heated by extremely hot rocks, which may have been close to molten. Engineers realised that this natural heat could become a source of electricity if they could reach the water and control what happened when it reached the surface.Drilling into the underground system released the pressure holding the hot water in liquid form. As that pressure dropped, the water began to boil, producing a mixture of water and steam. The mixture was brought upwards through the wells and separated at the surface.The dry steam was then sent through pipes to the power station, where it drove turbines to generate electricity. This process of allowing hot geothermal water to boil as its pressure falls is what gave Wairākei its pioneering flash-steam technology.The development was not simply a matter of finding hot water. Engineers had to create an entire system capable of bringing geothermal fluid out of the ground, separating the steam and directing it towards the turbines.The original steamfield bore, known as WK1 or WK001, became an important symbol of that early work. Although the well has since been cemented up, its wellhead remains intact. A commemorative plaque was installed there in 1985.Engineering New Zealand reports that the techniques developed during this early period of geothermal drilling helped establish methods that continue to influence geothermal well drilling. That makes the original bore more than a remnant of an old power project; it represents the experimental engineering that made the wider development possible.The scale of the underground resource also became apparent as the field developed. More than 50 wells are currently in production, with an average depth of more than 610 metres. The deepest reaches approximately 1,500 metres.Wairākei was the world’s second geothermal power station, but it achieved a major first by using flash steam from geothermal water as the energy source. It demonstrated that naturally heated underground water could be developed on a commercial scale rather than being treated simply as a geological curiosity.The station was first commissioned in 1958, but the development was not completed until 1963. Its construction represented years of work by scientists and engineers from New Zealand’s Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, the Ministry of Works and the Electricity Department.Their achievement was not limited to designing the buildings and turbines. The project required them to understand the geothermal field, develop wells, manage the steam and water coming from underground and create a reliable route from the resource to the generators.Wairākei did not remain a small experimental facility. The power station now consists of two powerhouses with installed capacities of 67.2 megawatts and 90 megawatts respectively.Together, they supply enough electricity to meet about 5% of the North Island’s electricity needs, as reported by Engineering New Zealand. The continuing presence of the geothermal field also keeps the relationship between the underground resource and the power station visible. Steam from wells in the Waiora Valley remains at the heart of the system, linking the modern operation to the drilling and engineering work that began decades ago.The heritage status describes the station’s success as a tribute to the scientists and engineers who conceived, designed, built and operated it. Their work showed how a natural resource beneath a volcanic landscape could be transformed into a dependable source of electricity.More than six decades after its first commissioning, the station remains a prominent example of how New Zealand’s volcanic landscape was turned into an opportunity for engineering innovation. What began with hot water beneath the ground became a pioneering power development and an enduring part of the country’s engineering history.
Article Summary: Wairākei Power Station in New Zealand changed the way geothermal heat could be turned into electricity when it was commissioned in 1958. Built beside the Waikato River, north of Taupō, the station drew on hot underground water beneath an active volcanic zone. Engineers drilled wells into the geothermal field and used the pressure of the heated water to produce steam for turbines. According to Engineering New Zealand, the project became the first in the world to use flash steam from geothermal water.

Article Title: 'Not invited': Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman on Brics Summit in Delhi
Article Text:
India is hosting the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi from September 12 to 13 at Bharat Mandapam

Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will not attend the Brics Summit in New Delhi after Dhaka said he was not invited to the two-day meeting.Bangladesh state minister for foreign affairs Humaiun Kobir said on Thursday there was scope for the country to send a government representative to the summit, but ruled out Tarique Rahman’s participation.“How shall we go? Has anyone from the Bangladesh government been invited? Our prime minister was not invited. Who told you that our Prime Minister was invited? The BIMSTEC Chair was invited. Then why are you asking this question?” he told reporters at the Foreign Service Academy, according to The Daily Star.Kobir said the invitation had been extended to the chair of the Bay of Bengal Initiative for Multi-Sectoral Technical and Economic Cooperation (BIMSTEC), rather than Bangladesh’s prime minister.India is hosting the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi from September 12 to 13 at Bharat Mandapam. The summit is being held under the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”.The meeting is expected to bring several international leaders and high-level delegations to the national capital.Ahead of the summit, Delhi Police has stepped up security across the city, with around 15,000 personnel and nearly 200 companies of paramilitary forces deployed for the event.“Police have been deployed in different sector zones across New Delhi. Drills have been conducted. CCTVs are being monitored. Meetings have been held with agencies... Our technical equipment has been installed so that any threat can be detected. We are ensuring that the public does not face any kind of inconvenience,” Sharma said.
Article Summary: India is hosting the 18th Brics Summit in New Delhi from September 12 to 13 at Bharat Mandapam. Delhi Police has stepped up security across the city, with around 15,000 personnel and nearly 200 companies of paramilitary forces deployed for the event.

Article Title: Trump's top advisors warn him Iran war could drag through end of his term: Report
Article Text:
Trump launched the conflict as an effort to pressure Iran over its nuclear programme.

Trump expects 'a quick end'

US-Iran fighting continues

Poll Vote & Share your view Do you believe the conflict with Iran will end before the midterm elections? Yes No 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Senior White House officials have privately warned US President Donald Trump that the war with Iran could continue for the rest of his presidency, despite his public prediction that the conflict will end soon after this year’s midterm elections, The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio were among the advisers who reportedly raised the possibility during private discussions with Trump in the Oval Office and Situation Room.According to the report, the officials told Trump that Iran could continue resisting US pressure, potentially keeping the conflict going until after the next US presidential inauguration in January 2029.Trump has publicly offered a much shorter timeline for the conflict. Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, he said he expected the war to end "immediately after" the US midterm elections in November. He argued that Iran was attempting to influence the election but would not be able to maintain its resistance for much longer."I think the war will end immediately after the election... They're desperate to try and affect the election so that we could get a nice, weak group of people in there and leave them alone and let them have their nuclear weapon."Trump has also indicated that diplomatic talks remain possible, although he has said negotiations are not his preferred option.Trump also referred to recent US strikes on Iran and attacks involving Iranian and American forces."We've knocked out nine of their ships; I would say that the attacks are caused by us — and you're going to see a lot more. We've taken our about nine of their tankers. Many of them are gone-zo."The US launched strikes on Iranian oil tankers during its latest offensive after Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps targeted US naval warships earlier this week.Iran has also retaliated, with multiple explosions reported over an American airbase in Jordan.Trump launched the conflict as an effort to pressure Iran over its nuclear programme. The first US strikes were carried out on February 28 as part of Operation Epic Fury, in coordination with Israel under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.The opening strikes killed Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, according to the material provided.The reported warning from Trump's senior advisers highlights the gap between the administration's private assessment of a potentially prolonged conflict and Trump's public expectation of a rapid end.
Article Summary: Senior White House officials have privately warned US President Donald Trump that the war with Iran could continue for the rest of his presidency. Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly raised the possibility during private discussions with Trump in the Oval Office and Situation Room. According to the report, the officials told Trump that Iran could keep resisting US pressure, potentially keeping the conflict going until after the next US presidential inauguration in January 2029.

Article Title: From voter ID to $5,000 cheques: Trump goes desi, mimics India’s election toolkit
Article Text:
Trump’s $5,000 dividend promise and push for voter ID suggest he is borrowing from India’s playbook of direct welfare and voter identification as electoral tools.

$5,000

Trump dividend

Trump cash push comes amid mounting US national debt which surpassed $40tn in August

US national debt has soared under Trump’s second administration.

From welfare to political technology

ID first, benefits later

Trump mid August had praised India’s election system and called for the passage of the SAVE America Act

A president under pressure

US President Donald Trump may never admit it, but it’s self-evident. The self-proclaimed oldest democracy is beginning to borrow from political toolkit of the world’s largest democracy.It first reflected in Trump’s obsession with photo identification for voting. Now comes the promise of money.It’s scene which is quite familiar for Indians. Come election time and it starts raining freebies for voters. The template works like this: Make promises first and then do economic calculations later, once you have won the polls.Now, something similar is happening in US.At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Trump offered voters a strikingly transactional proposition: Return Republicans to power in Congress and every adult American citizen could receive $5,000.“Pretend that I’m on the ballot just one more time,” Trump told supporters.“If the Republicans win the House of Representatives and the United States Senate...I will issue a dividend to every adult citizen in the United States of America for $5,000,” Trump said.“It will be called the Trump dividend,” the president said. “Now all we have to do is win.”With potentially more than 200 million payments, Trump could be promising well over $1 trillion in “dividends” unless the programme is restricted by income or other eligibility criteria, a WSJ report said.There is little chance that a $1 trillion-plus payout would sail through Congress at a moment when US public debt has surpassed $40 trillion for the first time and is already pushing up borrowing costs.But as political messaging, the promise matters. For anyone familiar with Indian elections, the formula feels instantly recognisable.Make voter identity a major political issue. Build databases capable of identifying citizens and beneficiaries. Deliver welfare directly rather than through opaque bureaucracies. Brand the benefit aggressively. And, most importantly, make sure the voter knows exactly which government put the money in the account.Trump, in other words, appears to be discovering the politics of Indian-style direct welfare.India’s welfare state has changed dramatically over the past decade. The Modi government’s Direct Benefit Transfer(DBT) changed that relationship.Money began arriving straight into bank accounts. A voter receiving Rs 2,000 directly into a bank account does not need a politician to explain government policy. That is electoral gold.Indian states took the idea further.Cash assistance for girls and women has become one of the most powerful electoral instruments in recent times.Madhya Pradesh’s Ladli Behna programme, Maharashtra’s Ladki Bahin scheme and similar initiatives elsewhere turned women not merely into welfare recipients but into a distinct political constituency.Indian politicians have understood that modern welfare is not merely about how much governments spend. It is about how clearly citizens can identify the sender.That is the political insight hiding inside Trump’s $5,000 proposal.However, Tump's dividend is not identical to India's DBT schemes: It targets no specific demographic and depends on a Congress that shows no appetite for it. But the underlying instinct is the same one Indian incumbents have refined: Convert a government or leader's flagging popularity into a direct, personal payment timed to the ballot box, and let voters decide whether to reward the giver.The other Indian parallel is Trump’s push for tougher voter identification. In his March 2025 executive order overhauling federal election procedures, Trump explicitly cited India and Brazil for linking voter identity to biometric databases, contrasting them with an American system that leans on self-attestation of citizenship.In August, Trump again posted on Truth Social about photo ID cards."We need to pass THE SAVE AMERICA ACT, now!" Trump wrote, invoking legislation that would mandate citizenship proof and government-issued photo ID for federal voting.His administration has repeatedly argued that US elections require stronger proof of identity and citizenship.However, India’s system is more complicated than that comparison suggests.The Electors Photo Identity Card, or EPIC, is widely used, but it is not the sole document voters can present. The Election Commission accepts several alternative photo identification documents, and Aadhaar is not mandatory for voting.The US also does not start from zero. Most states already have some form of voter identification requirement.Still, politically, Trump is assembling two ideas that sit comfortably together in the Indian political imagination: Prove who the voter is and then deliver benefits directly to that person.Trump has promised to campaign aggressively for Republicans and he is expected to make about 35 trips on behalf of candidates in closely fought races. He is also directing his political action committee to deploy some of the hundreds of millions of dollars it has raised in key contests, a Bloomberg report said.There is no doubt that Trump is feeling the heat. Polling shows Americans unconvinced by Trump's insistence that affordability complaints are overblown, and Wednesday's convention drew visible empty seats as vulnerable Republican candidates skipped the event altogether.Trump’s popularity is at all-time low and he has entangled US in what seems to be a forever war with Iran.But politically, the message is unmistakable. Faced with the prospect of losing Congress and spending the remainder of his presidency as a lame duck, Trump appears increasingly willing to borrow from India’s electoral playbook.
Article Summary: Donald Trump is borrowing from India's playbook of direct welfare and voter ID as electoral tools. At the Republican midterm convention in Dallas, Trump offered voters a strikingly transactional proposition: Return Republicans to power in Congress and every adult American citizen could receive $5,000.

Article Title: Sheikh Hasina's daughter Saima Wazed resigns from WHO post following fraud allegations
Article Text:
Her departure comes amid allegations of financial fraud and misrepresentation of her academic credentials

Poll Vote & Share your view What should be the WHO's priority when handling allegations involving senior officials? Ensuring a fair investigation Maintaining transparency Protecting institutional credibility Following due process 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s Southeast Asia regional director and daughter of ousted Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina , has resigned from her post following fraud investigations by the UN agency and Bangladeshi authorities, Reuters reported on Wednesday.Wazed’s resignation was confirmed in a resignation letter seen by Reuters. Her departure comes amid allegations of financial fraud and misrepresentation of her academic credentials, which she has denied.The WHO placed Wazed on unpaid administrative leave after Bangladesh’s Anti-Corruption Commission filed cases against her in March 2025, alleging fraud, forgery and misuse of power. She was first sent on leave in July 2025.The WHO later accused Wazed of "committing financial fraud in relation to her travel to China" and of misrepresenting her academic credentials, according to a July 3, 2026, letter from her lawyers to the WHO seen by Reuters.Wazed’s removal from her WHO role had previously been welcomed by Bangladesh’s interim government as a step towards accountability. "We view this as an important first step toward accountability," then-chief adviser’s press secretary Shafiqul Alam had said in 2025."We firmly believe that a permanent resolution is necessary, one that removes Saima from her position, revokes all associated privileges and restores integrity to this prestigious role and the credibility of the UN system as a whole," he had said.The development comes as Bangladesh continues to seek the extradition of Hasina and other Awami League leaders from India. New Delhi has said the request is being "examined as part of our established processes".
Article Summary: Saima Wazed, the World Health Organization’s Southeast Asia regional director and daughter of ousted Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, has resigned from her post. Her departure comes amid allegations of financial fraud and misrepresentation of her academic credentials, which she has denied.

Article Title: 'Make ground in Gaza tremble': Egypt warned Netanyahu of Hamas plans before October 7
Article Text:
Details emerge on Egypt’s warning to Netanyahu

Fresh details have emerged about warnings issued to Israel ahead of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack, amid a report that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was warned by the United Arab Emirates about plans for a major assault in the weeks leading up to the invasion.The latest information also sheds further light on previously reported warnings from Egyptian intelligence officials during the same period.According to Army Radio, the Shin Bet intelligence service conveyed to Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu warnings from its Egyptian counterparts that Hamas intended to “make the ground in Gaza tremble.”The Egyptian side provided only a general warning, without offering any specific details.In the days following the October 7 onslaught, an Egyptian intelligence official said Jerusalem had ignored repeated warnings that the Gaza-based terror group was planning “something big,” including an apparent direct warning from Cairo’s intelligence minister to Netanyahu, as cited by Times of Israel.According to the report, then-Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar assessed that the warning referred, at least in part, to Hamas seeking to raise the issue of kidnapped Israeli researcher Elizabeth Tsurkov in talks with Israel over a potential hostage deal.Shortly before the warning was issued, Hamas and Iraqi Shiite militia Kataeb Hezbollah, the group holding Tsurkov, had reportedly agreed that she would be treated as a Hamas asset in negotiations with Israel.The talks would involve the release of a large number of terrorists in exchange for the handover of two Israeli captives and the bodies of two IDF soldiers held in Gaza.The development comes as a new investigative report by Israeli newspaper Haaretz claimed that UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed had warned Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that then-Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar was preparing a “major attack” against Israel. Netanyahu, however, reportedly did not share the warning with Israel’s senior security leadership.Around 10 days after their reported conversation, Hamas launched its October 7, 2023, attack on Israel.The Haaretz report is based on the new book Kidnapped: 843 Days of Abandonment, which claims that bin Zayed spoke to Netanyahu for 45 minutes from Abu Dhabi. During the conversation, bin Zayed also reportedly urged Netanyahu to address broader sources of instability, including Gaza’s economic situation and rising tensions in the West Bank.According to a UAE presidential adviser interviewed for the book, bin Zayed was “surprised” by Netanyahu’s response, saying the Israeli prime minister did not appear “alarmed”.However, Netanyahu's office has rejected the claims made by the report.In a post on X, the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office said that any exchange of relevant information between the two countries took place solely through intelligence channels.“The press reports are false. No warning was given to the Prime Minister by the United Arab Emirates before October 7. If there was any relevant information, it was passed through intelligence channels between the two countries,” it posted.
Article Summary: Details emerge about warnings issued to Israel ahead of October 7, 2023, Hamas attack. Israel's Shin Bet intelligence service warned that Hamas intended to ‘make the ground in Gaza tremble’ Egyptian intelligence official said Jerusalem had ignored repeated warnings that the Gaza-based terror group was planning ‘something big’

Article Title: 'What exactly is funny?': Mamdani and AOC under fire for 'grinning' at 9/11 ceremony
Article Text:
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and democratic representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez participate in a memorial on the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, Friday, Sept. 11, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Pamela Smith)

New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani Democratic represenative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez found themselves in the middle of controvorsey on Friday after a camera briefly captured them sharing a light moment at the 9/11 memorial.The footage shows a young man sobbing at the memorial while names of the victims were being read, then it cuts to Mamdani and Cortez who appear to be grinning during a conversation. However, their conversation wasn’t audible.This comes after relatives of 9/11 victims garnered more than one lakh signatures, asking Mamdani to not attend the Friday event, citing him appointing Ramzi Kassem as the New York's chief legal counsel. Kassem had represented Al-Qaeda operative Ahmed al-Darbi, who pleaded guilty to war-crimes charges.Steve Guest, a former senior staffer for Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, called the exchange "disgraceful," adding that "AOC and Mamdani look happy."However, Michael Ragusa, a member of former Mayor Rudy Giuliani's security detail pushed back on the framing of the clip."The videos of [them] laughing are not true. I was standing next to them the whole time", tweeted Ragusa, according to WPIX-11."The camera just caught her greeting him hello. Multiple other politicians were laughing and joking behind me. Republicans and Democrats", he added.The Pittsburgh Republican Committee pointed to the moment on X as an example of why 9/11 victims' families had objected to Mamdani's presence in the first place, and former Los Angeles mayoral candidate Spencer Pratt also weighed in publicly.Closer to home, City Councilwoman Inna Vernikov, R-Brighton Beach, said she was angered by what she saw, arguing that Mamdani showed up despite thousands of families of terror victims asking him to stay away, only to be seen laughing as families around him wept. "This is NYC's Mayor," she said.Republican representative Randy Fine, a frequent critic of democratic socialists and of opponents of Israel, went further still, referring to the mayor as "Jihad Mamdani" and arguing that neither he nor Ocasio-Cortez belonged anywhere near Ground Zero.Former Trump White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson posed a simpler question: "What exactly is funny?"The context of Mamdani and Cortez’s conversation remains unknown.
Article Summary: New York City mayor Zohran Mamdani and Democratic represenative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez found themselves in the middle of controvorsey on Friday. A camera briefly captured them sharing a light moment at the 9/11 memorial. The footage shows a young man sobbing at the memorial while names of the victims were being read, then it cuts to Mamdhani and Cortez who appear to be grinning during a conversation.

Article Title: 'Married brother to bring him into USA': DHS probing Ilhan Omar's family immigration history
Article Text:
DHS secretary Mullin says investigation into Ilhan Omar's immigration history is ongoing over allegation she married her brother to help him enter the US.

The allegations against Omar

DHS’s statement

US Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin has revealed new details about an ongoing investigation into Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar’s immigration history, saying federal authorities are examining allegations that she married her brother to help him enter the United States.Speaking to conservative commentator Benny Johnson at the Republican National Convention in Dallas on Thursday, Mullin claimed investigators were looking beyond Omar’s disputed marriage allegation and examining her family’s broader immigration history.“We know that she married her brother to try to bring him into the United States,” Mullin said, adding that there “may be more to this” and that investigators were looking into possible “illegal activity” related to the family’s entry into the US.Mullin said the matter remained an “ongoing investigation” and insisted authorities would act only if they found evidence of wrongdoing.The allegations centre on Omar’s 2009 marriage to British citizen Ahmed Nur Said Elmi. Conservative critics have alleged that Elmi was Omar’s biological brother and that the marriage was entered into to facilitate his immigration to the US.Omar has repeatedly denied the allegation, saying Elmi was not her brother and rejecting claims that she committed immigration fraud.The allegations gained national attention in 2019 after then-President Donald Trump and conservative groups called for an investigation. They have resurfaced periodically amid political attacks on the Minnesota Democrat.However, the allegation has never been established in court. No federal agency has publicly released findings proving that Elmi was Omar’s brother or that the marriage was entered into for immigration purposes.Mullin said investigators were examining whether false information had been provided during the immigration process and suggested that potential violations could still be pursued years after they allegedly occurred.“If we actually move a case forward, it's not a political case,” Mullin said. “It's an actual case because they did things wrong.”The DHS did not confirm the specific allegations to news agency Newsweek upon asking. A department spokesperson said the agency does not comment on specific investigative techniques, ongoing investigations or potential future actions, adding: “No one, including members of Congress, are above the law.”Mullin did not provide documentary evidence during the interview to support his assertion that Omar married her brother, nor did he identify any charges being considered against her.Previous reporting has raised questions about aspects of Omar’s marriage history but has not established the central allegation.The Star Tribune examined records and communications related to Omar’s marriages in 2019 and reported discrepancies involving the timeline of her marriages and divorces. The reporting did not establish that Elmi was her brother.The New York Times also examined the allegations and reported that while questions had been raised about Omar’s personal history, there was no publicly available evidence demonstrating that Elmi was her sibling.In May, US President Trump once again told a crowd that he believes Omar “married her brother, which is totally illegal.”Marriage fraud is a federal crime in the US, punishable by up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine.Omar has described the accusations as false and politically motivated.
Article Summary: US Homeland Security secretary Markwayne Mullin revealed new details about an ongoing investigation into Democratic Representative Ilhan Omar’s immigration history. Mullin said federal authorities are examining allegations that she married her brother to help him enter the US. Omar has repeatedly denied the allegation, saying Elmi was not her brother.

Article Title: US diesel prices cross $6 a gallon amid Iran war
Article Text:
Representative image

Diesel prices in the US hit yet another record Friday, soaring past $6 a gallon on average as Washington's war with Iran disrupts the world's flow of fuel. The national average of nearly $6.06 is up from $5.85 last week and almost $3.71 this time last year, according to motor club AAA.Higher diesel prices mean more expensive transportation for a long list of everyday goods. That's because diesel is used for many freight and delivery networks. And some businesses have already passed along steeper costs to consumers in the form of added fees on online orders and packages in the mail.Prices at the pump for diesel and regular gasoline - which hit nearly $4.30 on average in the US Friday - closely follow those of crude oil. And oil has renewed its rise recently. This week, both Brent, the international standard, and US crude surpassed $100 a barrel for the first time in months as fighting between the US and Iran escalated again. AP
Article Summary: The national average of nearly $6.06 is up from $5.85 last week and almost $3.71 this time last year, according to motor club AAA. This week, both Brent, the international standard, and US crude surpassed $100 a barrel for the first time in months.

Article Title: As US marks 25 years of 9/11, victims' kin hit out at Saudi, former presidents
Article Text: Relatives of those killed in the 9/11 attacks on Friday called out Saudi Arabia for alleged complicity in the carnage - and chided past US presidents in attendance at a remembrance ceremony for failing to call Riyadh to account.The Sept 11, 2001, attacks were carried out by mostly Saudi hijackers and orchestrated by mastermind Osama bin Laden , a wealthy Saudi who founded al-Qaida. Washington maintains strong military and diplomatic ties with the kingdom.The annual reading of the names of the victims at the National 9/11 Memorial in New York is a sombre ceremony and is usually entirely apolitical, making the comments especially jarring. "You are missed more with each year that passes, but how can it be 25 years and still we have no justice for the role that Saudi Arabia played in your murder?" Tom Strada's widow Terry, the national chair of 9/11 Families United, said in her remarks."Yes, we finally made it into a court and have proved that the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia fomented a rancid culture of anti-American terrorism around the globe, and then sent its agents to support the radical Islamist hijackers so they could attack you and all of our loved ones," she said, to applause from the audience. Strada was referring to a lawsuit brought against Saudi Arabia's authorities by 9/11 Families United that alleges the kingdom supported the attackers.She then took aim at US leadership, as former presidents George W Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden looked on, along with current Vice President JD Vance. "For 25 years, administration after administration - including leaders in front of us here today - chose to protect the Saudis instead of standing with a 9/11 family," Strada said, calling for action from President Donald Trump, who skipped the event. "President Trump can still change that. Tell the Saudis to stop lying. Tell them that if they want to be friends with the USA, they cannot continue to deny all of this, all of the pain, all of the destruction that we have all been suffering through," she added. "Vice President Vance, thank you for being here today. Please carry that message back."Bill Clinton was beside other past presidents at Ground Zero in New York, but his two White House terms predate the attacks.After Strada's remarks, another of those reading names of the fallen, the nephew of victim Lisa Marie Terry, accused "the deep state" of having "hidden the truth about what happened that day 25 years ago." "President Trump, you're our last hope. Release the unredacted files that implicate Saudi Arabia, while what's left of the victims' families are still alive to see it," he said.Trump observed the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks at a ceremony at the Pentagon by commemorating the lives lost when al-Qaida militants hijacked planes and killed nearly 3,000 people in three locations and upended American foreign policy and national security.Trump and first lady Melania Trump listened as the names of the 184 people killed at the Pentagon that day were read aloud, a bell tolling between each. In his remarks, Trump recounted the stories of several of the victims and insisted that the moment has led to a fortification of American resolve. "We will never, ever forget," Trump said. "That's why we fight today. We don't have a choice." Earlier, in a downpour at daybreak, defence secretary Pete Hegseth and top military officials stood outside and watched as a giant American flag was unfurled on the building struck by one of those planes a quarter-century ago. agencies
Article Summary: Relatives of 9/11 victims call out Saudi Arabia for alleged complicity in the carnage. They chided past US presidents in attendance for failing to call Riyadh to account. The annual reading of the names of the victims is a sombre ceremony and is usually apolitical.

Article Title: Indian-origin investor's H-1B prediction: If 10% of Indians stuck in US Green Card backlog return, India’s GDP could rise 1%
Article Text:
Indian-American entrepreneur says US's loss would be India's gain if even 10% of those stuck in Green Card backlog go back to India.

H-1B debate adds to uncertainty

But will these Indians return?

Indian-American entrepreneur Vivek Wadhwa said if Indians waiting for residency in the US go back to India as America First activists want them to, it will be India's gain. India could get a major economic boost if skilled Indians caught in the US green-card backlog begin returning home, Wadhwa predicted, arguing that the return of even a fraction of them could add 1% to India's GDP over the next two to three years.Wadhwa made the prediction in a post on X while discussing the growing debate over H-1B visas and the possibility of skilled Indian workers leaving the US amid tightening immigration policies. The US administration moved towards eliminating the 60-day grace period for H-1B visa holders in the latest move. If this proposal becomes a rule, then H-1B visa holders and their family members will be out of legal status in the US the day the H-1B visa holder loses their job. Now, H-1B visa holders get 60 days to plan for the future after layoff but in the new proposal, the last day in the job would also be the last day in the US.“With all the debates about H-1Bs and sending skilled Indians back, here’s my prediction: this could add 1% to India’s GDP over the next 2–3 years alone,” Wadhwa wrote.Wadhwa said more than one million Indians are stuck in America's green-card backlog. If just 10% of them return to India, he estimates that would mean around 100,000 highly skilled workers coming back with their savings, professional experience and networks.“Imagine if 20% or 30% returned,” he wrote, suggesting the economic impact could be considerably larger.Wadhwa's argument is that a reversal of that migration could give India access not only to skilled workers but also to people who have spent years building careers in the US and accumulated capital, business connections and knowledge of the American market.“The flow is already in reverse,” Wadhwa wrote, describing the potential movement of Indian professionals back to their home country as a possible turning point.He argued that India could turn what is being viewed as a setback for Indian immigrants in the US into an economic opportunity. “America's loss could become India's biggest economic gain,” he wrote.Wadhwa's comments come as the US immigration system faces renewed debate over H-1B visas and employment-based immigration.He has previously called for the H-1B programme to be scrapped and replaced with a new skilled-immigration system, arguing that the programme has been undermined by labour arbitrage, so-called body shops and long green-card backlogs.In August, Wadhwa argued that the US should move away from a system that leaves skilled immigrants dependent on employers and instead create an immigration framework that gives talented workers greater freedom to change jobs and launch companies.His latest post takes that argument a step further, suggesting that restrictions and uncertainty in the US could accelerate a reverse brain drain, with experienced Indian professionals choosing to build their careers and businesses in India.Many social media users argued that Wadhwa's premise is wrong, as Indians stuck in the US GreeCard queue would prefer to explore European countries instead of going back to India. "It’s a mistaken belief. Who would come here with taxes so high , poor water and air quality and C grade civic infrastructure. I have engaged with lot of them and they all are planning to shift to some European country / Canada / Australia," one wrote.
Article Summary: Indian-American entrepreneur says US's loss would be India's gain if even 10% of those stuck in Green Card backlog go back to India. Vivek Wadhwa says the return of even a fraction of them could add 1% to India's GDP over the next two to three years.

Article Title: In 1950, Long Beach opened Veterans Memorial Stadium; sold to its city college for $1 in 1987, it is now being replaced by a $250 million, 285,453-sq-ft sports complex
Article Text:
Multi-purpose sports centre to bring facilities together

Demolition marks end of local sports era

Long Beach City College has broken ground on a $250 million stadium and sports complex, starting a major redevelopment that will replace its 76-year-old Veterans Memorial Stadium with a modern 285,453-square-foot sports precinct. The redevelopment was officially launched during a groundbreaking ceremony at the college's Liberal Arts Campus. The historic stadium will be demolished to make way for a new regional sports hub, which is expected to open in summer 2029. According to official announcements from Long Beach City College and reports by local news outlet Long Beach Patch, the new 18-acre complex will include a 10,000-seat outdoor stadium, a 2,500-seat indoor arena, specialised track and field facilities, and dedicated football and soccer fields. The project is being funded through Measure LB, an $850 million facilities bond approved by local voters in 2016 to upgrade campus infrastructure. Veterans Memorial Stadium first opened in 1950 under city ownership before it was transferred to Long Beach City College for just $1 in 1987. For about seven decades, the 11,600-seat concrete venue served as an important sports and community centre across Southern California.The new 285,453-square-foot sports complex has been designed to bring athletic activities together in one location. Previously, many of the college's sports facilities were spread across different parts of the Liberal Arts Campus. Along with the main 10,000-seat outdoor stadium and 2,500-seat indoor arena, the project will include training facilities, sports medicine and rehabilitation areas, kinesiology classrooms, administrative offices, basketball and volleyball courts, concession stands and a Hall of Champions honouring former student-athletes. “Veterans Memorial Stadium has been part of our community's fabric for more than 75 years, and as a former Viking football player, I know how personal this place is to so many of us,” said Uduak-Joe Ntuk, President of the Long Beach Community College District Board of Trustees, in a press statement issued by the college. “It has served as a gathering place for students, families, athletes, veterans, and the broader community. With the support of local voters through Measure LB, we have an opportunity to preserve that spirit and write a new chapter for Long Beach City College and the community we serve.”Dr Mike Muñoz, Superintendent-President of Long Beach City College, said the new facilities would benefit both students' academic and athletic development. “This groundbreaking marks a major step forward in how we support our student-athletes at Long Beach City College,” Dr. Muñoz noted in the press release. “This new complex will give our students access to modern athletic and instructional spaces designed to support their success both in competition and in the classroom. What matters most is what our students will be able to accomplish here, and I look forward to seeing how this investment helps them reach their full potential.” Project managers also plan to seek Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) Gold certification for the complex. The project will include energy-efficient power systems, recycled materials and sustainable water management.The stadium's history dates back to 1945, when 17 local soldiers serving in the South Pacific wrote to city officials asking for a stadium dedicated to local residents killed during World War II. The venue opened five years later in 1950 and soon became more than just a sports facility. During its seven decades of operation, Veterans Memorial Stadium served as the home of the Long Beach City College Vikings and Long Beach Polytechnic High School football teams. It also hosted regional track meets, high school graduation ceremonies, motorcycle races, roller derby, rugby matches, swap meets and commercial film shoots. The redevelopment began with site clearance and structural demolition. Architecture firm Gensler is designing the new complex, while Swinerton is the general contractor responsible for the first phase of demolition. Cordoba Corporation is managing the overall project for the college district. During construction, local high schools and college sports teams that regularly used the stadium will move their competitions and graduation ceremonies to other regional facilities.
Article Summary: Long Beach City College has broken ground on a $250 million stadium and sports complex. The redevelopment will replace its 76-year-old Veterans Memorial Stadium with a modern 285,453-square-foot sports precinct. The new 18-acre complex will include a 10,000-seat outdoor stadium, a 2,500-seat indoor arena and dedicated football and soccer fields. The project is being funded through Measure LB, an $850 million facilities bond approved by local voters in 2016.

Article Title: In 2025, Connecticut student Vihaan Kamath started selling homemade cookies for charity; by August 2026, his nonprofit had raised $66,331 and helped nearly 1,000 children
Article Text:
Connecticut teen Vihaan Kamath turns homemade cookies into a $66,000 charity mission. (Photo: St.Jude)

Teen’s cookie fundraiser grows into $66,000 nonprofit

Vihaan Kamath uses homemade cookies to raise money for children’s charities. (Photo: St. Jude)

From home kitchen to nonprofit

Teen baker’s nonprofit has helped nearly 1,000 children since launching in 2025. (Photo: St. Jude)

$20,000 raised in the first year

From his kitchen to a growing nonprofit, Vihaan Kamath is baking for a cause. (Photo: St. Jude)

St. Jude becomes a key part of his mission

Teen plans to keep nonprofit going after college

A Connecticut teenager has turned his love of baking into a growing nonprofit that has raised more than $66,000 to support children in need.Vihaan Kamath, 16, a Greenwich-area high school student preparing to enter his senior year, founded Cookie for a Cause in April 2025. The nonprofit sells homemade cookies and directs its proceeds toward children’s charities, including St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital and Yale New Haven Children’s Hospital.What began as a small fundraising idea has since grown into an initiative that has helped nearly 1,000 children with medical care, school supplies and everyday necessities.According to St. Jude, Kamath initially began raising money through cookie sales after returning from a summer trip to India, where he had spent time with his grandmother, whom he calls “anama.”During visits to Mumbai, Kamath accompanied his grandmother as she carried out charitable work in schools and hospitals. He remembers helping distribute notebooks and pencils to children and visiting the pediatric cancer ward at Tata Memorial Hospital, where he saw families who had travelled long distances seeking lifesaving treatment for their children.“That stuck with me through the years,” Kamath said.Those experiences eventually inspired him to find a way to support children in need in both India and the United States.Because Kamath already enjoyed baking with his mother and grandmother, he decided cookies could become the foundation of his fundraising efforts.Chocolate chip and sugar cookies became his specialties. He initially approached local businesses and corporations, offering his baked goods in exchange for donations to children's causes.“I just kept reaching out to more people and local businesses and partnered with a few different people,” he said. “People really seemed to have an interest in it.”His parents, Ravish and Vijaya Kamath, helped by providing ingredients including flour, sugar, eggs and chocolate chips.“It is their way of contributing to my cause,” Vihaan said.In April 2025, he formally established Cookie for a Cause as a nonprofit, with proceeds going to charity. He created a website where customers could place orders and continued baking most of the cookies in his home kitchen.For larger orders, he has occasionally used a local pastry shop, whose owner and employees have supported his efforts and offered advice on improving his recipes.The fundraiser quickly exceeded Kamath’s expectations.Between April and December 2025, Cookie for a Cause raised approximately $20,000.“From April 2025 to December 2025, we raised $20,000, which is phenomenal. I didn't even think we were going to get that far,” Kamath said.The nonprofit has since continued to grow. Kamath has now raised $66,331 and has set an ambitious target of $100,000 by the end of 2026.His father initially thought the project might eventually fade as his son balanced schoolwork and sports, but he soon realized that Kamath was committed to making it a long-term effort.“I didn’t know how far he would go with this,” Ravish Kamath said. “It was surprising, but he started to get on social media channels for this and then started to reach out to local businesses. It is now something considerable that he has done.”Kamath eventually expanded his fundraising to support children in the United States and connected with St. Jude Children’s Research Hospital.“I found St. Jude to be one of the best places to partner with and help out,” he said.He was later accepted into the St. Jude Leadership Society, a program that gives high school students an opportunity to develop leadership skills while raising funds and awareness for children treated by St. Jude.His connection with St. Jude also has roots in his experiences in India. Tata Memorial Hospital is part of the St. Jude Global Alliance, which brings together institutions around the world to improve care for children with cancer and other catastrophic diseases.Kamath has no plans to stop baking once he graduates from high school.He wants to study business in college and has already begun building a student team that can continue Cookie for a Cause after he leaves for university.“I created a student board with sophomores and freshmen from my school who will continue this after I move,” he said. “I’ll continue it when I go to college.”His goal is to create an organization that can continue growing even when he is no longer running its day-to-day operations.“I don’t want to stop,” Kamath said, adding that he hopes younger students can eventually take over different aspects of the nonprofit “so that this keeps growing.”
Article Summary: Connecticut teen Vihaan Kamath, 16, founded Cookie for a Cause in April 2025. The nonprofit sells homemade cookies and directs its proceeds toward children’s charities. It has helped nearly 1,000 children with medical care, school supplies and everyday necessities.

Article Title: Elon Musk reacts to Irish man's discovery that he would have to wait for 14 years to get Indian citizenship
Article Text:
Elon Musk reacts to a viral post about getting Indian citizenship.

What was the social media post all about

Aidan Joyce, a social media account that claimed to be an Irish man, said he fell in love with India and wanted to make Kolkata his home. He asked Elon Musk 's AI chatbot Grok how he could move to the country permanently. The exchange caught the attention of Elon Musk, who reacted to the discussion on X with a brief assessment of India's immigration system: “India is realistic. ”The Irish man, who had apparently been visiting Kolkata with his family, asked Grok about the possibility of becoming an Indian citizen. He wanted to know how quickly he could settle in the country and eventually obtain citizenship.Grok's response, however, made clear that moving to India permanently would not be an easy or quick process.According to the exchange shared online, the man was told that obtaining Indian citizenship could take at least 14 years, depending on his circumstances and the route he takes. He would first need to establish legal residence in India and meet the requirements for naturalisation.The answer also pointed out that India generally does not allow dual citizenship, meaning someone who becomes an Indian citizen would have to give up their existing citizenship."Wow that's a long time. Look, here is the story, I arrived with my partner and 2 children. Can we get some social welfare while we try and get a job. I'm totally skint at the moment, so I need a few $$ fast. How much will the Indian state pay us while we wait. Tell me briefly please," Joyce asked Grok. "None. India has no cash social welfare or unemployment payments for new arrivals or non-citizens. Ration cards, pensions and most assistance require Indian citizenship plus eligibility (e.g. BPL status). Formal-sector schemes need prior contributions. Support yourselves," the chatbot replied.Then Joyce asked if he could quickly buy a house in India and the answer was 'no'.The post was meant to be a reality check for Indians who have been in the waiting line for Green Cards for years. It also showed that India does not offer any welfare and while visa holders can buy houses in the US, it is not so easy in India. But what started as a mockery turned into Elon Musk's endorsement for the Indian system."Hilarious thread of Irish guy asking about moving to India. It takes 12 years for citizenship, you must renounce previous passports, of course zero welfare -- they'll just deport you," one commented. Musk said India's system is realistic.
Article Summary: Aidan Joyce, a social media account that claimed to be an Irish man, said he fell in love with India and wanted to make Kolkata his home. He asked Elon Musk's AI chatbot Grok how he could move to the country permanently. The exchange caught the attention of Elon Musk, who reacted with a brief assessment of India's immigration system.

Article Title: A 27-year-old Tennessee diesel mechanic wanted to farm full-time; solar sites gave his sheep 400+ acres to graze, letting him quit his job and build a 300-ewe flock
Article Text:
High land prices make farming difficult for young producers

Solar grazing creates benefits for both sides

Solar grazing expands across the US

A 27-year-old Tennessee diesel mechanic has left his job to become a full-time livestock farmer after gaining grazing access to more than 400 acres of utility-scale solar farms. The arrangement, made through vegetation management contracts at solar sites, allowed the young farmer to expand his flock to more than 300 breeding ewes without having to buy the large amount of land usually needed for a commercial sheep operation. According to regional advocacy group Appalachian Voices, solar grazing, also known as agrivoltaics, is creating new opportunities for small livestock farmers across the American South. The practice involves using sheep to control grass and weeds growing beneath and around ground-mounted solar panels. Solar companies avoid using fuel-powered mowing equipment, while farmers gain access to fenced pasture through long-term grazing agreements.Finding enough affordable pasture remains one of the biggest challenges for people trying to start commercial livestock farms in the United States. In East and Middle Tennessee, rising land prices and suburban growth have pushed the cost of farmland beyond the reach of many young farmers.Those without inherited family property or large amounts of capital can struggle to purchase enough acreage to make livestock farming financially viable. High equipment costs and expensive land rentals can also force young farmers to keep full-time jobs outside agriculture. That often leaves farming as a smaller side business rather than a full-time career. Solar farms can provide another option through vegetation management agreements. Developers usually surround their facilities with strong fencing and may install water systems. They also plant grass and clover between rows of solar panels, creating pasture that can be used by grazing animals. Sheep can then be brought onto the site to keep vegetation under control. Keeping grass below the lower edge of the solar panels helps prevent plants from interfering with the panels while avoiding the need for heavy mowing equipment. Using sheep also reduces the risk of machinery damaging solar equipment. Tractors and mowers can potentially strike panels, support structures or other equipment, while sheep can graze around the installations without causing the same risks.Sheep grazing on solar farms is becoming a growing partnership between renewable energy companies and local farmers. Research and reporting by Appalachian Voices found that solar operators can reduce vegetation maintenance costs by using local shepherds to manage grass and weeds. Farmers, meanwhile, receive access to pasture and an additional source of income. Sheep are particularly suited to solar facilities because of their size. Unlike cattle and horses, sheep can move under relatively low solar panel structures and graze around steel support posts. Their smaller size also allows them to reach areas where standard mowing equipment may have difficulty operating safely. For the Tennessee producer, income from vegetation management contracts provided the financial security needed to leave his diesel mechanic job and work full-time with his livestock. Access to more than 400 acres of solar pasture gave him enough space to grow his breeding flock to more than 300 ewes. The large area also made rotational grazing possible. Under this system, sheep are moved between different fenced sections of pasture, giving grass time to recover. Rotational grazing can also help reduce parasite pressure by preventing animals from repeatedly grazing the same areas.The growth of sheep grazing on solar farms in Tennessee is part of a wider trend across the US renewable energy industry. Data from the American Solar Grazing Association shows that livestock are now being used to manage vegetation across tens of thousands of acres of solar installations in the country. Sheep grazing is being used at utility-scale solar facilities in more than two dozen states. The practice is creating additional contract income for livestock farmers while providing solar companies with an alternative to conventional vegetation management. Agrivoltaic sites can also provide environmental benefits. Reported benefits include higher organic matter in topsoil, better water retention and lower emissions from mowing equipment.
